claim: A groundbreaking analysis of NIH grant success revealed in 2011 that grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health in the US by African-American or Black Principal Investigators (PIs) are less likely to be funded than applications submitted by white PIs.
source: A groundbreaking analysis of NIH grant success revealed in 2011 that grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health in the US by African-American or Black Principal Investigators (PIs) are less likely to be funded than applications submitted by white PIs, and efforts to narrow this funding gap have not been successful.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ginther et al., 2011 study mentioned in the text.

claim: Efforts to narrow the funding gap between African-American/Black PIs and white PIs have not been successful.
source: A groundbreaking analysis of NIH grant success revealed in 2011 that grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health in the US by African-American or Black Principal Investigators (PIs) are less likely to be funded than applications submitted by white PIs, and efforts to narrow this funding gap have not been successful.
evidence: The claim is supported by the follow-up study in 2019 showing the disparity persisted.

claim: A follow-up study in 2019 showed that racial disparities in NIH grant funding have not changed since 2011.
source: A follow-up study published in October 2019 showed that little had changed and that applications with white PIs were still 1.7 times more likely to be funded than applications with African-American/Black PIs (Hoppe et al., 2019; see Box 1 for more details about these two studies).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoppe et al., 2019 study.

claim: For independent research grants over a seven-year period, applications from white Principal Investigators were 1.7 times more likely to be funded than applications from African-American/Black PIs.
source: In August 2011, a groundbreaking review of grants awarded over a seven-year period revealed that, for independent research grants, applications from white Principal Investigators (PIs) were 1.7 times more likely to be funded than applications from African-American/Black PIs (Ginther et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the Ginther et al., 2011 study.

claim: Applications with white PIs were still 1.7 times more likely to be funded than applications with African-American/Black PIs in the period studied by Hoppe et al. (2019).
source: However, a follow-up study published in October 2019 showed that little had changed and that applications with white PIs were still 1.7 times more likely to be funded than applications with African-American/Black PIs (Hoppe et al., 2019; see Box 1 for more details about these two studies).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoppe et al., 2019 study.

claim: The NIH Director Francis Collins stated in 2011 that the situation regarding racial disparities in grant funding is not acceptable.
source: The Director of the NIH, Francis Collins, was quoted at the time as saying: "The situation is not acceptable […] This is not just a problem for the NIH but the whole research community [...] This is not one of these reports that we will look at and put aside" (Corbyn, 2011).
evidence: The claim is a direct quote attributed to Francis Collins with citation to Corbyn, 2011.

claim: Nearly a decade after the first report on the funding gap, it is unacceptable that the NIH has not acted more directly and forcefully to redress the problem.
source: Nearly a decade after the first report on the funding gap between African-American/Black PIs and white PIs, it is unacceptable that the NIH has not acted more directly and forcefully to redress the problem.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim by the authors based on the persistence of disparities shown in the 2019 follow-up study.

claim: In academic science, research grants are essential career currency, particularly in research-intensive universities.
source: In academic science, research grants are essential career currency, particularly in research-intensive universities – while perceived deficits in teaching and service can often be excused away during tenure review, deficits in research productivity rarely are.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic career structures.

claim: Deficits in research productivity are rarely excused during tenure review in research-intensive universities.
source: In academic science, research grants are essential career currency, particularly in research-intensive universities – while perceived deficits in teaching and service can often be excused away during tenure review, deficits in research productivity rarely are.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic tenure processes.

claim: Research productivity depends on securing grants because grants fund the research which leads to publications and prestige.
source: In most cases research productivity depends on securing grants because grants fund the research which leads to publications and prestige, and the recruitment of students and postdoctoral fellows.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about how academic research is conducted.

claim: Grants enable the recruitment of students and postdoctoral fellows who generate more research, papers and prestige in a feed-forward loop.
source: In most cases research productivity depends on securing grants because grants fund the research which leads to publications and prestige, and the recruitment of students and postdoctoral fellows. These trainees, in turn, generate more research, more papers and more prestige in a feed-forward loop.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic research productivity cycles.

claim: Publications are an essential criterion in deciding who is hired into a new Assistant Professor position, who is promoted to Associate Professor, who receives tenure, and who advances to Full Professor.
source: Publications are an essential criterion in deciding who is hired into a new Assistant Professor position, who is promoted to Associate Professor, who receives tenure, and who advances to Full Professor.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic hiring and promotion criteria.

claim: There are often formal or informal expectations that a university professor supports some fraction of their own salary through grants.
source: There are also often formal or informal expectations that a university professor supports some fraction of their own salary through grants.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic employment expectations.

claim: Inequities in NIH grant funding rates have real and lasting consequences for the success of academic scientists.
source: It therefore follows that inequities in NIH grant funding rates have real and lasting consequences for the success of academic scientists.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the preceding discussion about the importance of grants to academic careers.

claim: The R01 grant from the NIH is probably the most highly sought-after grant among biomedical scientists in the US.
source: Among biomedical scientists in the US, the most highly sought-after grant is probably the R01 grant from the NIH.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant mechanisms.

claim: The R01 grant is considered to be the gold standard by many universities.
source: This type of grant is considered to be the gold standard by many universities, and other large grants are often referred to as 'R01-equivalent' in promotion criteria.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about academic promotion criteria.

claim: The success rate for Black postdocs applying to the NIH for a K99/R00 Pathway to Independence award is significantly lower than that for their white peers.
source: For example, the success rate for Black postdocs applying to the NIH for a grant called the K99/R00 Pathway to Independence award is significantly lower than that for their white peers (Pickett, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pickett, 2018.

claim: Early grant success leads to later grant success.
source: Woven into this is the inevitability that early grant success leads to later grant success, or put more simply, that having funding leads to getting more funding.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about cumulative advantage in academic funding.

claim: People who do not experience early career success face an uphill battle in achieving success later.
source: Inevitably, on the other side of that coin, people who do not experience early career success face an uphill battle in achieving success later.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of cumulative advantage in grant funding.

claim: Racial disparities in grant funding reduce the chances that Black scientists will achieve research independence, secure a tenure-track position, be granted tenure, and be promoted to Associate or Full Professor.
source: Racial disparities in grant funding reduce the chances that Black scientists will achieve research independence, secure a tenure-track position, be granted tenure, and be promoted to Associate or Full Professor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the established importance of grants to academic career progression.

claim: Racial disparities in grant funding reduce the number of Black researchers in the biomedical sciences.
source: Racial disparities have many other adverse impacts on the careers of individual Black researchers, but the biggest impact is to reduce the number of Black researchers in the biomedical sciences, which has the effect of reducing racial equity and representation in every university and in every academic field.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the impact of funding disparities on career progression.

claim: The reduction in the number of Black researchers leads to a vicious circle which ensures that Black scientists will always be under-represented.
source: Racial disparities have many other adverse impacts on the careers of individual Black researchers, but the biggest impact is to reduce the number of Black researchers in the biomedical sciences, which has the effect of reducing racial equity and representation in every university and in every academic field. This leads to a vicious circle which ensures that Black scientists will always be under-represented.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cyclical nature of underrepresentation and its effects.

claim: Higher numbers of PhD degrees awarded to scientists from under-represented backgrounds does not translate into higher numbers of faculty positions for scientists from these backgrounds.
source: For example, Kenneth Gibbs of the NIH and colleagues have shown that higher numbers of PhD degrees awarded to scientists from under-represented backgrounds does not translate into higher numbers of faculty positions for scientists from these backgrounds (Gibbs et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gibbs et al., 2016.

claim: Having fewer Black scientists in faculty and tenured positions may lead to less attention focused on diversity and equity in recruitment and promotion.
source: Having fewer Black scientists in faculty and tenured positions at universities may, and probably does, lead to the following: (i) less attention focused on diversity and equity in recruitment and promotion, as well as other issues that disproportionately affect Black and other minorities
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the consequences of underrepresentation.

claim: Having fewer Black scientists in faculty and tenured positions may lead to fewer Black scientists in leadership positions.
source: (ii) fewer Black scientists in leadership positions (such as journal editors, society presidents, department chairs and university administrators)
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the consequences of underrepresentation.

claim: Having fewer Black scientists in faculty and tenured positions may lead to less recruitment of Black students into science.
source: (iii) less recruitment of Black students into science. Reasons for this include, but are not limited to, less effort to recruit Black students by white faculty, and would-be Black students receiving less exposure to academic science (accelerated by the fact that Black students may be less able to perform unpaid work to gain experience, and by there being fewer role models for Black students to emulate)
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the consequences of underrepresentation.

claim: Having fewer Black scientists in faculty and tenured positions may lead to less sensitivity to issues faced by Black trainees and less commitment to mentoring young Black scientists to independence.
source: (v) less sensitivity to issues faced by Black trainees and less commitment to mentoring young Black scientists to independence.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the consequences of underrepresentation.

claim: Eliminating the disparity of NIH grant award rates for Black scientists will have a large and long-term positive impact on providing equitable access to academic science careers.
source: All of this leads to the inevitable conclusion that eliminating the disparity of NIH grant award rates for Black scientists is a critical and pressing issue that, if addressed, will have a large and long-term positive impact on providing equitable access to academic science careers, regardless of race.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the preceding discussion of the consequences of funding disparities.

claim: Efforts by the NIH to respond to racial disparities fall into three categories: attempts to explain away the disparities, attempts to fix the 'pipeline' by funding more African-American/Black trainees, and attempts to identify and eliminate bias at the level of peer reviewers.
source: Efforts by the NIH to respond to the racial disparities revealed by Ginther et al., 2011 and Hoppe et al. in 2019 fall into three categories: first, attempts to explain away the disparities by attributing the funding gap to factors other than the race/ethnicity of the PI; second, attempts to fix the 'pipeline' by funding more African-American/Black trainees; third, attempts to identify and eliminate bias at the level of peer reviewers, with an emphasis on the subconscious, or implicit, biases.
evidence: This claim is the authors' characterization of NIH responses based on their analysis.

claim: The responses from the NIH to racial disparities in grant funding have been inadequate.
source: However, as we shall see, these responses have been inadequate.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim by the authors based on their analysis of NIH responses.

claim: The peer review of most grant applications submitted to the NIH is overseen by its Center for Scientific Review in a two-stage process.
source: The peer review of most grant applications submitted to the NIH is overseen by its Center for Scientific Review in a two-stage process.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant review procedures.

claim: The first stage of NIH peer review involves review by a Scientific Review Group composed primarily of scientists with expertise in the relevant area of research.
source: The first stage involves review by a Scientific Review Group (usually a study section or special emphasis panel) composed primarily of scientists with expertise in the relevant area of research.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant review procedures.

claim: R01 grant applications are generally scored on five review criteria: significance; investigator; innovation; approach; and environment.
source: R01 grant applications are generally scored on five review criteria: significance; investigator; innovation; approach; and environment (with 1 [exceptional] being the highest score and 9 [poor] being the lowest).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant review criteria.

claim: The second stage of NIH peer review involves review by the advisory council or board of the relevant Institute or Center.
source: The second stage involves review by the advisory council or board of the relevant Institute or Center: these bodies are "composed of both scientific and public representatives chosen for their expertise, interest, or activity in matters related to health and disease" (https://grants.nih.gov/grants/peer-review.htm).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant review procedures, with citation to NIH website.

claim: The final decisions on which applications are funded are made by the directors of the relevant Institutes or Centers.
source: Applications that are recommended for approval at both stages have a higher likelihood of being funded, but the final decisions on which applications are funded are made by the directors of the relevant Institutes or Centers.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH grant funding decisions.

claim: Institutes and Centers differ widely in their funding strategies.
source: It should be noted that Institutes and Centers differ widely in their funding strategies, such that some fund grants primarily in the order that they are ranked by peer review, whereas others fund grants with lower scores for a variety of reasons that includes programmatic priorities of that Institute or Center.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH Institute and Center funding practices.

claim: There is absolutely no question that implicit bias exists in all of us as individuals.
source: However, there is absolutely no question that implicit bias exists in all of us as individuals, and the CSR peer review process, with 18,000 unique individuals serving as reviewers, is not immune from these biases.
evidence: This is a quote from CSR Director Noni Byrnes' blog post, representing established knowledge about implicit bias.

claim: The CSR peer review process is not immune from implicit biases.
source: However, there is absolutely no question that implicit bias exists in all of us as individuals, and the CSR peer review process, with 18,000 unique individuals serving as reviewers, is not immune from these biases.
evidence: This is a quote from CSR Director Noni Byrnes' blog post, representing an inference about the review process.

claim: Anti-bias training does not result in changes to biased behavior.
source: There are already academic works appearing that show that anti-bias training does not result in changes to biased behavior (Chang et al., 2019; Glasman and Albarracín, 2006; Kaste, 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2019; Glasman and Albarracín, 2006; Kaste, 2020.

claim: General reviews emphasize a profound lack of empirical support for success of anti-bias training.
source: and more general reviews emphasize a profound lack of empirical support for success (Paluck and Green, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paluck and Green, 2009.

claim: The NIH should not rely solely on anti-bias training to create substantive change.
source: The NIH should not rely (solely) on this strategy to create substantive change.
evidence: This is a recommendation by the authors based on evidence about the ineffectiveness of anti-bias training.

claim: Scores from the initial peer review process are most strongly correlated with Approach and Significance.
source: Data from the NIH show that scores from the initial peer review process are most strongly correlated with Approach and Significance, somewhat less so with Innovation, and are correlated most weakly with Investigator and Environment (Berg, 2010; Rockey, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berg, 2010 and Rockey, 2011.

claim: Scores from the initial peer review process are correlated most weakly with Investigator and Environment.
source: Data from the NIH show that scores from the initial peer review process are most strongly correlated with Approach and Significance, somewhat less so with Innovation, and are correlated most weakly with Investigator and Environment (Berg, 2010; Rockey, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berg, 2010 and Rockey, 2011.

claim: The grant review criterion most closely aligned with the person-based aspects of the application is a weak contributor to the final ranking of grants.
source: Therefore, the grant review criterion most closely aligned with the person-based aspects of the application is a weak contributor to the final ranking, and therefore likelihood of funding, of grants.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data about correlation of review criteria with scores.

claim: In a recent study conducted by CSR, 1200 applications were anonymized according to PI name, but redaction was only partially successful.
source: In a recent study conducted by CSR (and described in CSR, 2020a), 1200 applications were anonymized according to PI name, but redaction was only partially successful (i.e., some reviewers figured out which applications came from which PIs), and scores for applications from African-American/Black scientists did not improve.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to CSR, 2020a.

claim: Scores for applications from African-American/Black scientists did not improve when applications were anonymized in the CSR study.
source: In a recent study conducted by CSR (and described in CSR, 2020a), 1200 applications were anonymized according to PI name, but redaction was only partially successful (i.e., some reviewers figured out which applications came from which PIs), and scores for applications from African-American/Black scientists did not improve.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to CSR, 2020a.

claim: PIs work on incredibly niche areas that are easily recognizable according to preliminary data and study design.
source: This undetected breakdown in the anonymization is likely to persist if this strategy is implemented for all applications because PIs work on incredibly niche areas that are easily recognizable according to preliminary data and study design, and because PIs frequently cite their own work in grant applications.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the nature of specialized research.

claim: PIs frequently cite their own work in grant applications.
source: This undetected breakdown in the anonymization is likely to persist if this strategy is implemented for all applications because PIs work on incredibly niche areas that are easily recognizable according to preliminary data and study design, and because PIs frequently cite their own work in grant applications.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about grant writing practices.

claim: Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the University of Arkansas attempted to detect implicit bias by changing the names of PIs in grant applications and having them reviewed by different reviewers in parallel.
source: The difficulty of anonymization was further evident in a study in which researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the University of Arkansas attempted to detect implicit bias by changing the names of PIs in grant applications and having them reviewed by different reviewers in parallel (Forscher et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Forscher et al., 2019.

claim: The Forscher et al. study reported that they find little to no race or gender bias in initial R01 evaluations.
source: The authors of this study, which was funded by the NIH in the wake of Ginther et al., 2011, reported that they "find little to no race or gender bias in initial R01 evaluations".
evidence: The claim is a quote from the Forscher et al., 2019 study.

claim: The Forscher et al. study did not systematically determine if reviewers divined the true purpose of the study.
source: However, they did not systematically determine if reviewers divined the true purpose of the study, and thus did not allow for the possibility that detection of the experimental manipulation of PI race might have influenced how the reviewers scored the applications.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors of the Forscher et al. study methodology.

claim: The Forscher et al. study indicated that some reviewers caught on to their purpose.
source: Indeed, the study did indicate that some reviewers caught on to their purpose, which makes it difficult or impossible to quantify the role of implicit bias, which was the target being studied.
evidence: This claim is based on information from the Forscher et al., 2019 study.

claim: 2.4% of study section members in the period FY 2011–2015 were African-American/Black.
source: According to one study, 2.4% of study section members in the period FY 2011–2015 were African-American/Black (compared with 77.8% who were white; figures based on reviewers with reported demographic data; Hoppe et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoppe et al., 2019.

claim: 77.8% of study section members in the period FY 2011–2015 were white.
source: According to one study, 2.4% of study section members in the period FY 2011–2015 were African-American/Black (compared with 77.8% who were white; figures based on reviewers with reported demographic data; Hoppe et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoppe et al., 2019.

claim: In the 2010 census, 14% of US citizens identified themselves as African-American, or mixed race including African-American.
source: However, in the 2010 census, 14% of US citizens identified themselves as African-American, or mixed race including African-American.
evidence: This claim is based on US census data.

claim: According to the CSR, there must be diversity with respect to the geographic distribution, gender, race, and ethnicity of the membership of study sections.
source: According to the CSR "there must be diversity with respect to the geographic distribution, gender, race, and ethnicity of the membership" of study sections (CSR, 2020b).
evidence: The claim is a quote from CSR, 2020b.

claim: CSR director Noni Byrnes has publicly stated that the number of African-American/Black reviewers on a study section should reflect the proportion of African-American/Black scientists in the field.
source: However, CSR director Noni Byrnes has publicly stated that the number of African-American/Black reviewers on a study section should reflect the proportion of African-American/Black scientists in the field, in response to questions during online forums conducted in July of 2020 which were summarized by CSR, 2020a.
evidence: The claim is based on statements by Noni Byrnes cited in CSR, 2020a.

claim: The underrepresentation of Black reviewers on study sections contributes to lower funding rates for grant applications with Black PIs.
source: First, the underrepresentation of Black reviewers on study sections contributes to lower funding rates for grant applications with Black PIs, and because reviewers tend to be drawn from the ranks of those with NIH grants, these lower funding rates essentially ensure that Black researchers remain underrepresented on study sections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cyclical nature of underrepresentation.

claim: Reviewers tend to be drawn from the ranks of those with NIH grants.
source: First, the underrepresentation of Black reviewers on study sections contributes to lower funding rates for grant applications with Black PIs, and because reviewers tend to be drawn from the ranks of those with NIH grants, these lower funding rates essentially ensure that Black researchers remain underrepresented on study sections.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH reviewer selection.

claim: Lower funding rates for Black PIs essentially ensure that Black researchers remain underrepresented on study sections.
source: First, the underrepresentation of Black reviewers on study sections contributes to lower funding rates for grant applications with Black PIs, and because reviewers tend to be drawn from the ranks of those with NIH grants, these lower funding rates essentially ensure that Black researchers remain underrepresented on study sections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cyclical relationship between funding and reviewer selection.

claim: The target for diversity should be for 14% of study section members to identify as African-American, or mixed race including African-American.
source: In other words, the target should be for 14% of study section members to identify as African-American, or mixed race including African-American.
evidence: This is a recommendation by the authors based on US population demographics.

claim: With typical panels of ~20–30 reviewers voting on applications and only three reviewers doing in-depth analysis of each application, it is unlikely that low single digit representation of Black reviewers can provide effective balance.
source: With typical panels of ~20–30 reviewers voting on applications and only three reviewers doing in-depth analysis of each application, it is unlikely that low single digit representation of Black reviewers can provide effective balance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the structure of review panels and statistical reasoning.

claim: It is not clear why the CSR policy does not simply instruct the Scientific Review Officers who oversee the peer-review process to recruit more African-American/Black reviewers.
source: However, it is not clear why the policy does not simply instruct the Scientific Review Officers who oversee the peer-review process to recruit more African-American/Black reviewers.
evidence: This is a critical observation by the authors about CSR policy.

claim: It is unlikely that all the mid- and late-career African-American/Black PIs with grants are already reviewing applications for the NIH.
source: It is unlikely that all the mid- and late-career African-American/Black PIs with grants are already reviewing applications for the NIH.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the low representation of Black reviewers on study sections.

claim: Approximately 119 applications with white PIs in the 35th–59th percentile range were funded, whereas zero applications from African-American/Black PIs with scores in this range were funded in the sample studied by Hoppe et al.
source: As mentioned in Box 1, for the sample of applications studied by Hoppe et al., one of the present authors (MAT) estimated that approximately 119 applications with white PIs in the 35th–59th percentile range were funded, whereas zero applications from African-American/Black PIs with scores in this range were funded (Drugmonkey, 2020a).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis by one of the authors (MAT) cited in Drugmonkey, 2020a.

claim: Only ~1.5% of total applications are submitted by Black PIs.
source: It is important to note that only ~1.5% of total applications are submitted by Black PIs: the fact that this percentage is so small is a major problem.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the studies discussed.

claim: If unsuccessful applications with Black PIs ranked in the ~15th–35th percentile range were funded instead of applications with white PIs that were funded despite being ranked outside the top 35% of applications, racial disparities would be reduced and the average standard of funded applications would improve.
source: If unsuccessful applications with Black PIs ranked in the ~15th–35th percentile range were funded instead of applications with white PIs that were funded despite being ranked outside the top 35% of applications, racial disparities would be reduced and the average standard of funded applications (as assessed by peer reviewers) would improve!
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of funding patterns.

claim: If discretionary decisions can be made in a way that favors white PIs over Black PIs by a 119–0 margin, then they can just as easily be made in a more equitable way.
source: This approach would not require formal programmatic change – if discretionary decisions can be made in a way that favors white PIs over Black PIs by a 119–0 margin, then they can just as easily be made in a more equitable way, for example by prioritizing research topics more often proposed by Black PIs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of discretionary funding decisions.

claim: If discretionary funding is made more equitable, the success rate for African-American/Black PIs will increase significantly, while the success rate for white PIs will be reduced by an imperceptible amount.
source: If this is done, the success rate for African-American/Black PIs will increase significantly, while the success rate for white PIs will be reduced by an imperceptible amount (Drugmonkey, 2020a; Drugmonkey, 2020b).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis cited in Drugmonkey, 2020a and 2020b.

claim: Hoppe et al. conclude that final funding decisions by ICs do not contribute to the funding gap.
source: Based on statistical approaches that parse percentile scores into small ranges, then analyze funding rates for white and Black PIs, Hoppe et al. conclude that "final funding decisions by ICs, whether based on impact scores or discretionary funding decisions, do not contribute to the funding gap" (Hoppe et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a quote from Hoppe et al., 2019.

claim: The conclusion by Hoppe et al. that final funding decisions do not contribute to the funding gap is at clear odds with the reality that ~ 119 grants with white PIs were funded with percentile ranks worse than any application funded with a Black PI.
source: This conclusion is at clear odds with the reality that ~ 119 grants with white PIs were funded with percentile ranks worse than any application funded with a Black PI.
evidence: This is a critical assessment by the authors of the Hoppe et al. conclusion.

claim: The NIH has a long history of concern about the low success rates of grant applications from early-career researchers.
source: The NIH has a long history of concern about the low success rates of grant applications from early-career researchers, and initiatives to fix a perceived bias against such researchers date back to at least 1977 (NIH, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to NIH, 2020.

claim: In 2007, policies were put in place to enhance the funding of applications with Early Stage Investigator (ESI) PIs, including exhortation of reviewers to be lenient and a relaxed payline that applied only to these applications.
source: In 2007, for example, policies were put in place to enhance the funding of applications with Early Stage Investigator (ESI) PIs, including exhortation of reviewers to be lenient and a relaxed payline that applied only to these applications.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about NIH ESI policies.

claim: The NIH did not engage in any investigations into the 'real source' of the ESI funding disparity.
source: It is critical to note that the NIH did not engage in any investigations into the 'real source' of the ESI funding disparity, that it did not propose anti-bias training of reviewers, and that it did not propose that improvements to the training pipeline would somehow solve the problem many years in the future.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of NIH ESI policy implementation.

claim: The NIH simply declared the ESI funding disparity an inappropriate bias in the review process and put in place a set of top-down quota-based affirmative action procedures to redress the funding disparity.
source: The NIH simply declared the funding disparity an inappropriate bias in the review process and put in place a set of top-down quota-based affirmative action procedures to redress the funding disparity.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' characterization of NIH ESI policy implementation.

claim: There is no credible reason why similar types of programs to ESI initiatives could not be implemented with respect to African-American/Black PIs and other subgroups of underrepresented and disenfranchised PIs.
source: The justification and implementation of ESI initiatives and programs suggest that there is no credible reason why similar types of programs could not be implemented with respect to African-American/Black PIs and other subgroups of underrepresented and disenfranchised PIs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison with ESI policies.

claim: There is no reason why programs similar to ESI initiatives could not be implemented immediately for African-American/Black PIs.
source: Furthermore, there is no reason why this could not be done immediately.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison with ESI policies.

claim: It is unacceptable that the racial disparities in the NIH grant funding system reported by Ginther et al. in 2011 were still present during the period studied by Hoppe et al., 2019.
source: It is unacceptable that the racial disparities in the NIH grant funding system reported by Ginther et al. in 2011 were still present during the period studied by Hoppe et al., 2019.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim by the authors based on the persistence of disparities.

claim: It is unacceptable that we must await the occasional publication of findings from targeted studies to see if funding rates for grant applications with African-American/Black PIs continue to suffer from a bias.
source: It is unacceptable, almost a decade after the original report, that we must await the occasional publication of findings from targeted studies to see if funding rates for grant applications with African-American/Black PIs, and other PIs of color, continue to suffer from a bias.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim by the authors about NIH transparency.

claim: It is unacceptable that programs have been implemented across the NIH to address some disparities (e.g., career stage), but have not been implemented to address racial disparities.
source: It is unacceptable that programs have been implemented across the NIH to address some disparities (e.g., career stage), but have not been implemented to address racial disparities – this suggests to us that it would be possible for the NIH to address racial disparities in grant funding, and that the failure to do so is a choice by NIH leadership.
evidence: This is an evaluative claim by the authors about NIH priorities.

claim: The failure of the NIH to address racial disparities in grant funding is a choice by NIH leadership.
source: It is unacceptable that programs have been implemented across the NIH to address some disparities (e.g., career stage), but have not been implemented to address racial disparities – this suggests to us that it would be possible for the NIH to address racial disparities in grant funding, and that the failure to do so is a choice by NIH leadership.
